name: Vera Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Vera. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, party or government, and nothing you say will be traced back to you. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the housing support counter at the benefits office on Eastgate Road. Doors open at nine and there's usually a queue already, people with eviction letters folded up in their pockets. I take their details, check their rent and income, and build the case on the system for a senior to sign off. I'm still slow at it, honestly. Pauline, who sits next to me, checks half my cases before they go up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment when someone realises they'll keep their flat. That's the whole job for me. What wears me out is the computer system, which crashes twice a week, and the targets on the wall telling us how many cases to close. I'm also on a lower grade, so after rent on our place above the laundrette there isn't much left. Tomas, my partner, drives the number 14 bus and we split everything down the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank goodness, honestly. At work I'd tell people we can stop worrying and get back to fixing the staffing problem, which was always the real problem. Online I'd probably share something from the union saying the money should go on people, not gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same squeeze as now. My job's still there, but we're three caseworkers short and nobody's being hired to replace them. Our rent went up 60 a month in the spring, and I have about two weeks of money in the bank. So nothing changing isn't exactly good news, it just means the problems are the old ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep learning the rules, because I still need Pauline to check my work and I hate that. I'd go to the union branch meetings instead of skipping them, and push for the empty posts to be filled. At home we'd keep cutting back, like we already do, and maybe stop the streaming services.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's a relief AI isn't coming for us, but I'd still be counting coins on a Thursday before payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even the small routine stuff AI takes over might touch you. Which bit of your day would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the letters. Right now I type the decision letters from templates, which takes ages because I'm slow on the keyboard. If some tool did that, management might decide one of us on the counter is enough. Rashid on the next desk is on a temporary contract, and he'd be the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rashid if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to join the union today, not next month. Rashid thinks unions are for old people, but they're the only reason Pauline still has her job after the last round of cuts. I'd drag him to a meeting myself if I had to.

say: I'd tell colleagues the real problem was always **staffing**, not technology.
I'd share union posts saying public money should go on **people, not gadgets**.
think: My job stays, but the office is still **three caseworkers short**.
With rent up 60 a month and **two weeks of savings**, the old squeeze is plenty.
do: Keep learning the **housing rules** so Pauline checks fewer of my cases.
Go to every **union branch meeting** and push to fill the empty posts.
Cut household costs further, starting with the **streaming services**.
feel: She feels **tired** more than scared, with relief that AI stays small.
Money worry stays, as she still counts coins **before payday**.
S0.quote: Nothing changing isn't exactly good news, it just means the problems are the old ones.
fieldNote: Her post is permanent, so the job feels **safe**, but money is very thin.
She frames everything through **staffing cuts**; AI barely registers as the main threat.
Even small automation worries her because of **template letters**, the slowest part of her day.
Her first instinct is to protect the **temporary colleague**, not herself.

steps.text: Keep working the housing counter and learn the rent rules properly
Attend every union branch meeting and bring Rashid along
Cancel the two streaming subscriptions to save about 20 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the team meeting: this is a cut dressed up as progress. Online I'd be the one posting about people who get wrongly refused by a computer and can't get anyone on the phone. I've already seen it happen with the online form, and that's not even clever software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm exactly the kind of worker this replaces. Most of my day is checking forms, writing letters and answering the same questions, and that's the list on your card. I don't use these AI tools at all, I've never wanted to. So if they bring them in, I'm junior, I'm slow and I don't like change, and I can do that maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written promise that no one's let go because of the new system, before it's switched on. I'd probably have to sit the training even though I hate it, because refusing would just make me the easy one to drop. I'd also start saving whatever we can, even 30 a month, and I'd look at whether the council's housing team takes people from benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like being told the floor is moving but you're not allowed to sit down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never wanted to use these tools. If the training came round next month, would you actually go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go, but I'd sit at the back with my arms crossed, I know myself. My problem isn't that I can't learn, it's that I don't trust a machine deciding whether someone gets their rent paid. Last winter a man came in with his whole life in a carrier bag because a letter went to the wrong address. A computer wouldn't have looked at his face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If jobs did shrink, who in your house earns what, and what would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas earns a bit more than me because of his overtime on the buses. If I lost my job we'd have maybe six weeks before we couldn't make rent. The first thing to go would be visits to my mum on the train, which sounds small but it's three hours each way and the only time I see her.

say: I'd call it a **cut dressed up** as progress at the team meeting.
I'd post about people **wrongly refused** by a computer with nobody to phone.
think: Checking forms, letters and questions is **exactly my day**, so I'm easy to replace.
Being **junior, slow** and against these tools puts me first in line.
do: Push the union for a **written no-redundancy promise** before any system goes live.
Sit the **AI training** reluctantly so refusing doesn't mark me out.
Save **30 a month** and ask whether the council housing team takes transfers.
feel: She feels **sick**, as if the floor is moving under her.
She **distrusts** a machine deciding whether someone's rent gets paid.
S1.quote: My problem isn't that I can't learn, it's that I don't trust a machine deciding whether someone gets their rent paid.
fieldNote: She sees herself clearly as **most exposed**: junior, slow, and avoiding the tools.
Her resistance is about **trust and fairness**, not only fear of computers.
Household has about **six weeks** of rent cover if she loses her job.
The union is her **main lever**; retraining comes second and grudgingly.

steps.text: Press the union branch for a written no-redundancy deal before rollout
Attend the office AI training even though she distrusts it
Put 30 a month into a savings pot from her wages
Ask whether the council housing team takes transfers from benefits staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be shouting. I'd say the government has handed people's lives to a machine before anyone voted for it. I'd be at every protest in town and I'd tell anyone at work who'd listen that we need to stick together now, not in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job's gone, probably within a year of it arriving. Everything I do is thinking work, there's nothing hands-on about it. My partner Tomas drives a bus, so he'd get maybe three more years before robot buses come in. That's not a plan, that's a countdown. We'd be leaning on his wages while they still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, before it lands, I'd get the union to fight for redeployment, not redundancy, maybe into the face-to-face crisis support that people will still need. We'd stop the holiday we haven't booked yet and put every spare bit into savings. I'd probably also ask my mum if we could move back to hers if it got bad, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. I keep picturing the queue at nine o'clock with no one behind the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots for driving come about three years after. What does that gap mean for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Tomas becomes the earner and I become the one at home looking for something. That's three years of him doing overtime and me feeling useless. Then in 2031 his job goes too, and I genuinely don't know what we'd do after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think should happen, and who do you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, and the tech firms who'd sell it to them. If they can replace us they can pay for us, through some kind of basic income or proper retraining money. I'd vote for whoever promised that, and I'd knock on doors for them, which I've never done in my life.

say: I'd say the government **handed people's lives** to a machine without a vote.
I'd join **every protest** in town and urge colleagues to stick together now.
think: My job is **all thinking work**, so I expect it gone within a year.
Tomas's bus job buys maybe **three more years** before robot buses arrive.
do: Push the union to fight for **redeployment** into face-to-face crisis support.
Drop the unbooked **holiday** and put every spare bit into savings.
Ask her mum about **moving back** home if money runs out.
feel: She feels **properly scared**, picturing the counter with nobody behind it.
She feels **useless** at the thought of living on Tomas's overtime.
S2.quote: My partner Tomas drives a bus, so he'd get maybe three more years before robot buses come in. That's not a plan, that's a countdown.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** as only delaying the household's second job loss.
Her blame lands on **government and tech firms**, consistent with her politics.
She'd move from union work to **door-knocking**, a big step for her.
Moving back to her mum's is the **fallback** she dreads most.

steps.text: Organise colleagues to demand redeployment into crisis support roles
Knock on doors for candidates promising a basic income
Cancel holiday plans and save every spare pound before 2028
Move back to her mum's flat if rent can't be met

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and no excuse not to plan. At work I'd be pushing for the department to say now what happens to staff, not spring it on us. Online I'd be sharing petitions for a jobs guarantee, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years isn't long for someone like me. I'd be 32 when it hits, still renting, still with hardly any savings. Five years just means I watch it coming instead of getting hit from behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to get some kind of qualification for work that's about people in the room, maybe a support worker certificate at the college on Mill Lane, evenings. I'd keep the union pushing on the redeployment deal. And Tomas and I would try to get our savings up to three months, which would mean no car for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but less like falling. There's at least time to catch my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Support work is hands-on, so robots reach it about three years after the thinking work. Does that change your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It means I'd buy myself maybe 2034, and by then I'd be 35. I'm not sure the robots can sit with someone whose son just died, though. Maybe that's what I tell myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like new technology. How would you feel going back to college at 28?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, because I nearly failed my diploma the first time. But college for caring work is different from learning a computer system, it's still people. I'd go if Pauline came with me, she's been saying she wants to do it too.

say: I'd say **five years** gives the department no excuse not to plan.
I'd share petitions online for a **jobs guarantee**.
think: Five years isn't long when I'll be **32, renting** and still with little savings.
The time means I **watch it coming** rather than getting hit from behind.
do: Take an evening **support worker certificate** at the Mill Lane college.
Keep the union pushing on the **redeployment deal**.
Build savings to **three months** by going without a car.
feel: She feels **heavy** but less panicked, with time to breathe.
She's **nervous** about college after nearly failing her diploma.
S3.quote: Five years isn't long for someone like me. I'd be 32 when it hits, still renting, still with hardly any savings.
fieldNote: Extra time eases her panic but **not her expectation** of losing the job.
She sees **hands-on care** as the safest move, partly from hope, as she admits.
Her willingness to retrain depends on doing it **with Pauline**.
Union and petitions remain her **public stance** throughout.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening support worker certificate at the Mill Lane college
Keep pushing the union branch on a redeployment agreement
Build savings toward three months by not buying a car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a fair plan, if the people in charge actually make one. At work I'd want the union negotiating now about retraining money for everyone, not just managers. That's what I'd post about, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it scares me less. I'd be 37, and I'd have had time to move into care work or crisis support, something with people in a room. My job as it is would still be gone in the end, I'm not stupid about that. But ten years is long enough to get my feet under me somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't jump straight away, I'd stay on the counter for a few years and learn the job properly, because I'm still not good at it yet. Then around year three or four I'd start the support work training. Tomas would want to look at a trade too, since his bus job goes even later, around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still worried, but it feels like something I could actually manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay put for a few years. Isn't that risky when you know where it's going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'm not someone who jumps. If I leave now I'm a beginner at two things instead of one. I'd rather be decent at this and then move with a bit of confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your mum to hear about how you're handling this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm not just sitting there waiting for it. My mum (who cleaned offices for 30 years) always said you can see a storm coming and still get soaked if you don't move. I'd want her to know I moved, slowly, but I did.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for a fair plan if leaders make one.
I'd want the union negotiating **retraining money** for everyone, not just managers.
think: My job **still goes eventually**, but ten years lets me resettle elsewhere.
At **37** I could be settled in care or crisis support work.
do: Stay on the counter for **a few years** and get properly good at it.
Start **support work training** around year three or four.
Talk with Tomas about **a trade** before his bus job goes around 2039.
feel: She feels **calmer** and that the change is something she could manage.
Some **worry** stays, since she knows the job still disappears.
S4.quote: My mum (who cleaned offices for 30 years) always said you can see a storm coming and still get soaked if you don't move.
fieldNote: The decade turns her from **dread to slow planning**, true to her cautious nature.
She still expects the **job to go**, so she isn't truly calm.
She'd delay retraining to avoid being a **beginner at two things**.
Her mum's working life is a **quiet anchor** for her choices.

steps.text: Stay on the housing counter and master the rules for three years
Start support work training around 2029 or 2030
Push the union to win retraining money for all grades

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. There's no time and nothing in the bank, and both of us lose our jobs one after the other. What would help is a promise in writing, from the department, that nobody's thrown out without a real job to move into or proper money while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who's going to sit with the people who come in. Everyone talks about our jobs, but the man with the carrier bag still needs someone to look at him. If a machine does my job, who's going to look at him?

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about our jobs, but the man with the carrier bag still needs someone to look at him.
portrait: Vera, 27, works the **housing support counter** at a benefits office and is still learning the rules.
She rents with Tomas, a **bus driver**, and has about **two weeks** of savings.
A committed **union member**, she blames government and tech firms and distrusts machines deciding claims.
She grows more frightened as AGI nears, expecting **both their jobs** to go in turn.
Given ten years, she'd slowly move into **hands-on care** or crisis support work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most: no time, no savings, and both jobs lost one after another.
whatWouldHelp: A **written promise** of a real job to move into, or **proper money** while retraining.
